title: Sabby Lewis's book and the Zanzibar with Ethel Waters and Don Redman
summary: Lewis bought arrangements from Tadd Dameron and others; at the Zanzibar they broadcast thrice nightly, backed Ethel Waters and shared the bill with Don Redman's intermission band.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it

blocks.x: What kind of a thing did he have going on?

Well he was an arranger and he was doin' things that the public liked. And he would buy music. He had Tadd Dameron write some things for him. He had a white fella...I understand he's a professor at some college in Brooklyn. His name was Jerry Hefron and he did a lot of the arranging. He had a good book, you know. When we were in New York at the Zanzibar, he had Freddy Webster in the band, Idrees Sulieman and George James...he used to be with Louis Armstrong years ago. We broadcast three times a night and that's when Leonard Feather heard me and that's when I started gettin' a little recognition, yeah.
So the work at the club Zanzibar was when you first went with Sabby Lewis?
And before you left for Boston? So about how long do you think that was that you were with him here in New York?

Oh, I don't know. I think we did about 16 weeks, I think. Yeah. And that was a great experience because I played Ethel Waters' act and I think we...I don't know if it was Broadway, it was a different situation and Joe Howard owned the place and it was really the big time. And I got to meet her pianist, Reginald Bean, who was a very gifted, gifted, gifted pianist and he was her accompaniest and we became quite friendly. I understand he works for ASCAP now. And Don Redman had the intermission band. Yeah. And he had Foots Thomas and his brother ...the other Thomas. And he had two tenors and I think it was Doc Cheatham playin' trumpet. He had a good band. Then this Latin flute player, I can't think of his name.* He came in with his intermission band, you know, playin' that Latin music, you know.
Then Dizzy would come by all the time and then...on my intermission I could run over to 52nd Street and hear everybody, then run back and hit the next show. It was exciting.
